(1) Vercel AI SDK: `ai` (package.json:82), `@ai-sdk/anthropic` (:48) and `@ai-sdk/openai` (:49). `git log -S 'from "ai"' -- lib app components` returns nothing, so they were never wired in: the app talks to providers over raw fetch through lib/ai/provider.ts and hand-rolls SSE in lib/ai/anthropic.ts:212 (`createAnthropicSseTranscoder`, consumed at app/api/v3/ai/chat/route.ts:342). The 19 apparent hits for `ai` are the string literal 'ai' used as a profile tab id (app/profile/page.tsx:79) and as a `scan_tags.source` value (lib/tags/auto-tags.ts:878). (2) `jsonwebtoken` (:91) and `@types/jsonwebtoken` (:122): the only mentions in source are a comment at lib/scanner/checks/code.ts:1736 and a UI label at lib/scanner/checks/page-checks/jwt.ts:140. The app's one real JWT verification, lib/auth/staff-oidc.ts:24, imports `jose`. (3) shadcn/v0 scaffold leftovers from the initial commit 26e639c5, none of which ever got a components/ui wrapper (there is no command.tsx, calendar.tsx, carousel.tsx, drawer.tsx, resizable.tsx, input-otp.tsx, sonner.tsx, form.tsx, accordion.tsx, collapsible.tsx, context-menu.tsx, hover-card.tsx, menubar.tsx, navigation-menu.tsx, radio-group.tsx, toggle.tsx or toggle-group.tsx in components/ui/): `@hookform/resolvers` (:50), `@neondatabase/serverless` (:51, named only as prose in app/docs/architecture/page.tsx), `@radix-ui/react-accordion` (:52), `-aspect-ratio` (:54), `-collapsible` (:57), `-context-menu` (:58), `-hover-card` (:61), `-menubar` (:63), `-navigation-menu` (:64), `-radio-group` (:67), `-toggle` (:76), `-toggle-group` (:77), `cmdk` (:86), `date-fns` (:87), `embla-carousel-react` (:88), `input-otp` (:89), `react-day-picker` (:101), `react-hook-form` (:103, no `useForm` or `FormProvider` anywhere), `react-resizable-panels` (:106), `sonner` (:110, the app uses components/ui/toaster.tsx over @radix-ui/react-toast) and `vaul` (:116). Separately `tslib` (:115) was added by commit b8bc8f83 'to resolve import error in react-remove-scroll'; react-remove-scroll@2.7.2 still declares `tslib: ^2.1.0` itself, so the direct entry buys nothing and only freezes the hoisted copy at an exact 2.8.1. Walking the lockfile closure, these twenty-five roots plus the two jspdf packages are the sole path to 78 packages totalling 77.6 MB installed, the largest being jspdf 28.8 MB, date-fns 10.4 MB, ai 6.4 MB, html2canvas 3.2 MB, @ai-sdk/openai 2.8 MB, @ai-sdk/anthropic 2.1 MB, dompurify 1.7 MB, pako 1.6 MB, undici 1.6 MB, canvg 1.3 MB and core-js 1.3 MB. core-js is also one of only three packages in the entire tree with `hasInstallScript: true`.
impact: Every production install and every Docker image layer carries 78 packages that no line of code can reach, which is 78 more npm accounts whose compromise would land executable code in the runtime of a security product. core-js arrives with a postinstall script purely because jspdf wants canvg. Operationally the list also misleads: a reader of package.json reasonably concludes there is a PDF export path, a Vercel AI SDK integration and a Neon serverless driver, and will go looking for all three. The jsonwebtoken entry is the sharpest edge, because a contributor adding a signed token has a JWT library already installed and one grep away that is not the vetted one (`jose`) the auth layer standardised on, so the wrong library gets used with no review signal.
recommendation: Delete those twenty-five entries, the two jspdf entries from AUDIT-012#fe-13 (package.json:92-93), and `@types/jsonwebtoken` (package.json:122) from `dependencies`/`devDependencies`, and drop `tslib` (:115) since react-remove-scroll pulls it transitively. Update the stale comment at tests/lib/reports/pdf-report.test.ts:8 that still references jspdf being in package.json. Also prune .github/dependabot.yml, whose `security` group (lines 59, 61, 64) and `scanning` group watch several of these. Regenerate package-lock.json on Linux or graft the entries by hand, per the lockfile-platform constraint this repo already documents: a Windows regeneration strips the Linux native bindings this lockfile currently has intact.

title: vitest and @vitest/coverage-v8 sit in dependencies, pulling 82 packages and a 20 MB rolldown native binary into the production graph, and the Dockerfile never passes --omit=dev so the devDependencies ship as well
description: This extends AUDIT-012#fe-13, which named the misplacement but attributed the cost to `npm ci --omit=dev` in the Docker build. This Dockerfile does not use that flag. Two separate mechanisms compound. First, `vitest` 4.1.11 (package.json:117) and `@vitest/coverage-v8` 4.1.11 (:81) are declared under `dependencies`, not `devDependencies`. Resolving the lockfile closure of the `dependencies` list with and without those two roots, 82 packages / 42.9 MB are reachable only through them: `@rolldown/binding-win32-x64-msvc` at 20.4 MB (on a Linux runner the equivalent `@rolldown/binding-linux-x64-gnu`), `vite` 8.2.2 with its own nested `lightningcss` 1.33.0 and full 11-platform native matrix at 9.1 MB for the local binary, plus @babel/types, @babel/parser, rolldown, magic-string, magicast, istanbul-reports, chai and the rest of the runner. That second lightningcss is a straight duplicate: @tailwindcss/node 4.3.3 already brings lightningcss 1.32.0 with its own full platform matrix, so the tree carries two copies of an 11-binary native package. Second, Dockerfile:24 runs `npm ci --silent --ignore-scripts` with no `--omit=dev`, and Dockerfile:77 then does `COPY --from=builder --chown=nextjs:nodejs /app/node_modules ./node_modules` into the runner stage. Measuring the lockfile's dev-flagged entries on disk gives 89 MB that is copied verbatim into the published ghcr image: typescript 23.2 MB, prettier 9.5 MB, lightningcss-win32-x64-msvc 9.1 MB, eslint-plugin-react-hooks 3.9 MB, axe-core 2.9 MB, eslint 2.8 MB, es-abstract 2.7 MB, @typescript-eslint/eslint-plugin 2.0 MB and so on.
impact: The published ghcr.io/vulnradar/vulnradar image ships a full test runner, a bundler with two native binaries, a TypeScript compiler, ESLint and Prettier into the runtime a self-hoster exposes to the internet. That is roughly 130 MB of pure image weight plus a much larger attack surface than the app needs, on a container that runs as a long-lived network service. It also means the fix AUDIT-012#fe-13 recommended (move the two packages to devDependencies) would not by itself shrink the image at all, because the Docker build installs dev dependencies unconditionally.
recommendation: Two changes, both one line. Move `vitest` and `@vitest/coverage-v8` from `dependencies` to `devDependencies` in package.json. Then change Dockerfile:24 to a two-stage install: keep `npm ci --ignore-scripts` in the builder (the build needs typescript and the tailwind toolchain) and, in the runner stage, replace the `COPY --from=builder /app/node_modules` at Dockerfile:77 with a separate `npm ci --omit=dev --ignore-scripts` layer, or add `RUN npm prune --omit=dev` in the builder after `npm run build` and copy the pruned tree. Either removes both the 89 MB of dev tooling and the 42.9 MB vitest subtree from the shipped image.

title: The overrides block forces ESLint 10 into three eslint-config-next plugins whose peer ranges stop at ESLint 9, and eslint.config.mjs already documents one total lint crash this caused
category: peer conflict papered over by an override
description: package.json:130 declares `eslint: ^10.9.0`. eslint-config-next 16.3.2 (package.json:131) declares `peerDependencies: { eslint: ">=9.0.0" }`, which ESLint 10 satisfies, but its own hard dependencies do not: the lockfile shows `node_modules/eslint-config-next/node_modules/eslint-plugin-import` 2.32.0 with `peerDependencies.eslint: "^2 || ^3 || ^4 || ^5 || ^6 || ^7.2.0 || ^8 || ^9"`, `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y` 6.10.2 with `"^3 || ^4 || ^5 || ^6 || ^7 || ^8 || ^9"`, and `eslint-plugin-react` 7.37.5 with `"^3 || ^4 || ^5 || ^6 || ^7 || ^8 || ^9.7"`. ESLint 10 is outside all three. The `overrides` block at package.json:146-154 forces it in anyway with three nested `{ "eslint": "$eslint" }` entries, which is what makes `npm ci` resolve instead of throwing ERESOLVE. That override is not cosmetic: eslint.config.mjs:47-55 documents the first thing it broke, in the repo's own words, 'eslint-config-next sets settings.react.version to "detect", which makes eslint-plugin-react probe the filesystem via context.getFilename(). ESLint 10 removed that legacy context method, so detection crashes the whole run', worked around by hardcoding `react: { version: "19.2.8" }` at eslint.config.mjs:55. Two more unguarded uses of removed ESLint 10 context APIs remain in the installed plugin (eslint-plugin-react/lib/rules/forward-ref-uses-ref.js:60 `context.getSourceCode()`, jsx-filename-extension.js:64 `context.getFilename()`); those two rules are off in core-web-vitals today, so they are latent rather than live. Running `npx eslint .` in the current working tree reproduces the failure class end to end: `TypeError: scopeManager.addGlobals is not a function at addDeclaredGlobals (node_modules/eslint/lib/languages/js/source-code/source-code.js:221)`, zero files linted, whole run aborted. To be precise about what that proves: this workspace's node_modules has drifted to eslint 10.8.1 while the lockfile pins 10.9.0, and CI on main is green, so this exact crash is not what CI runs. What it demonstrates is that the plugin set has no floor under it, because ESLint 10 patch releases are free to keep removing legacy APIs that three unsupported plugins still call.
impact: `npm run lint` is a required, merge-blocking CI job (.github/workflows/ci.yml, the `lint` job), and it depends on three plugins that upstream does not claim to support on this ESLint major. When one of them next touches a removed API, lint does not report findings, it aborts with a TypeError and zero files checked. The failure mode is the bad one: a crash that reports no problems reads, to anyone skimming, a lot like a clean run, and the repo has already had to hand-patch one instance of it inside eslint.config.mjs.
recommendation: Pick one of two. Either drop `eslint` back to `^9` in package.json:130 (which is what eslint-config-next 16.3.2's whole plugin set is tested against) and delete the three nested overrides at package.json:146-154, or keep ESLint 10 and stop depending on the unsupported plugins: replace `eslint-config-next/core-web-vitals` in eslint.config.mjs:13 with `@next/eslint-plugin-next`'s recommended rules plus `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` 7.1.1 (which is the one plugin in the set that already declares `^10.0.0` support) and configure jsx-a11y/import rules explicitly or not at all. Whichever is chosen, add a comment to the overrides block naming why it exists, since an override that silences a real peer conflict is invisible once ERESOLVE stops firing.

title: Severity ordering is redeclared in nine private tables under three mutually incompatible numeric conventions, two of which share the identifier SEVERITY_RANK, and the info label already differs between the app and the ~750 public /checks pages
description:
There is a canonical severity ordering: SEVERITY_PRIORITY at lib/config/constants.ts:628 (critical 5, high 4, medium 3, low 2, info 1), consumed with a `b - a` comparator by components/scanner/results-list.tsx:335, app/api/v3/demo-scan/route.ts:236, app/api/v3/scan/bulk/route.ts:252 and app/api/v3/scan/authenticated/route.ts:427. Eight further private tables encode the same idea:

Convention A, critical is 5 down to info is 1 (same as canonical): lib/scanner/dedupe.ts:18 `SEVERITY_RANK`, lib/reports/compliance-report.ts:37 `SEVERITY_RANK`.
Convention B, critical is 0 up to info is 4 (inverted): lib/ai/scan-summary.ts:47 `SEVERITY_RANK`, lib/ai/auto-tag-suggest.ts:136 `SEVERITY_RANK`, lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:78 `SEVERITY_ORDER`, lib/scanner/execute-crawl-scan.ts:73 `SEVERITY_ORDER`.
Convention C, info is 0 up to critical is 4 (a third numbering): lib/scanner/software-inventory.ts:715 `SEVERITY_RANK`.

So the identifier `SEVERITY_RANK` means three different things in five files, and the comparator direction flips with it: compliance-report.ts:150 sorts `severityRank(b) - severityRank(a)` while scan-summary.ts:77 and auto-tag-suggest.ts:166 sort `severityRank(a) - severityRank(b)`, and both are correct only for their own table. Lifting either constant into a shared module, or copying a comparator between these files, silently reverses the ordering with no type error, because every table is `Record<Severity, number>`.

The name `SEVERITY_ORDER` is separately overloaded: components/scanner/severity-badge.tsx:12 exports it as `readonly Severity[]` (consumed by six other components: results-list.tsx:345, dashboard.tsx:428, ai-choice-modal.tsx:154, ai-verify-result-modal.tsx:60, repos/page.tsx:49 and github-scan-result-modal.tsx:59), lib/reports/markdown-report.ts:23 declares another `Severity[]`, and execute-scan.ts:78 / execute-crawl-scan.ts:73 declare it as a numeric Record.

The label layer has already drifted user-visibly. components/scanner/severity-badge.tsx:71 (SEVERITY_TONE), lib/reports/markdown-report.ts:31 and lib/reports/compliance-report.ts:29 all label the lowest level "Info". lib/seo/seo-ui.tsx:25 labels it "Informational", and that is the SeverityPill rendered on app/checks/[id]/page.tsx and app/tools/api-scanner/page.tsx, which is the ~750-page public SEO surface. There are also two different components exported as `SeverityPill` (components/history/severity-pill.tsx:11, which delegates to severityTone(), and lib/seo/seo-ui.tsx:41, which inlines its own hsl alphas of 0.1/0.25 against SEVERITY_TONE's /15 and /40), plus four colour maps: components/scanner/severity-badge.tsx SEVERITY_TONE, components/docs/docs-types.ts:75 SEVERITY_COLORS, lib/reports/pdf-report.ts:18 SEVERITY_COLORS as RGB tuples, and lib/config/client-constants.ts:304 SEVERITY_COLORS, which has zero consumers.
impact: Today: the same info-severity finding reads "Info" in the product and "Informational" on the public check pages, and the same severity pill has two different tints depending on which surface renders it. Tomorrow: a developer who consolidates `SEVERITY_RANK` (a natural cleanup, since the name is already shared) or copies a working comparator between two of these files inverts a sort with no compile error, and findings list least-severe-first in a report, an AI summary, or the dedupe winner selection. lib/scanner/dedupe.ts:175 uses its rank to pick which duplicate finding survives, so an inversion there would keep the info-level copy and discard the critical one.
recommendation: Put one table in lib/config/client-constants.ts next to SEVERITY_LEVELS: keep SEVERITY_PRIORITY's convention (critical highest) and export both it and the ordered array. Delete the seven private tables and rewrite each comparator to `PRIORITY[b.severity] - PRIORITY[a.severity]`, checking each one's direction as you go (lib/ai/scan-summary.ts:77, lib/ai/auto-tag-suggest.ts:166, lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:712, lib/scanner/execute-crawl-scan.ts:220 and :585 all currently sort ascending against an inverted table). Rename lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:78 and lib/scanner/execute-crawl-scan.ts:73 out of the way first so `SEVERITY_ORDER` unambiguously means the array. Move SEVERITY_TONE's labels to that same module and have lib/seo/seo-ui.tsx:25 read them so "Info" is one string, and delete the unconsumed lib/config/client-constants.ts:304 SEVERITY_COLORS.

title: The documented 1 MiB request-body cap lives inside parseBody, which only 19 of the 73 body-reading routes use; the other 54 call request.json() directly and there is no global limit behind them
category: guard applied to a subset of siblings
description:
lib/api/api-utils.ts:170-176 documents the cap as a deliberate fix: "L-10: Hard cap on JSON request bodies. Without this, a client can send a multi-GB JSON body that the server will buffer before rejecting. 1 MiB is more than enough for our route shapes." It is enforced only inside parseBody (lib/api/api-utils.ts:181-228), which checks content-length against MAX_REQUEST_BODY_BYTES at :188-196 before calling request.json().

I split every route.ts under app/api by which one it uses. 19 files call parseBody, 54 call `request.json()` or `req.json()` directly, and the two sets do not overlap at all. The 19 are almost entirely under app/api/v3/auth/, app/api/v3/account/, plus keys, browser/sessions, admin/staff-invites and admin/updater/apply, which is the shape of a fix applied by directory and never extended. The 54 include the whole scan surface (app/api/v3/scan/route.ts, scan/bulk, scan/crawl, scan/verify-batch, scan/import-spec, scan/remediation/bulk), the whole teams and support-ticket surface, app/api/v3/admin/route.ts, app/api/v3/webhooks/route.ts, app/api/v3/domains/route.ts, and the two contact forms.

There is no backstop underneath them: I checked next.config.mjs and middleware.ts and neither sets a body size limit, and Next.js App Router route handlers have no default one (the Pages Router's 1 MB bodyParser limit does not apply). app/api/v3/account/unsubscribe/route.ts is in PUBLIC_PATHS (lib/config/public-paths.ts:178) and reads its body raw, so at least one uncapped route is reachable with no session.
impact: Any signed-in account (signup is open) can POST an arbitrarily large JSON body to app/api/v3/scan/route.ts or any of the other 53 routes and the server buffers it in memory before any validation runs. On a deployment sized for ~50 users, a few concurrent multi-hundred-megabyte bodies are enough to OOM the process. The narrower and more likely cost is maintenance: the cap is written down as a security requirement in one helper that 74% of the body-reading routes do not go through, so the requirement is not actually a property of the API.
recommendation: Do not try to convert 54 handlers. Add the content-length check to middleware.ts for any request to /api/ with a method that carries a body, using the same MAX_REQUEST_BODY_BYTES value exported from lib/api/api-utils.ts, and return 413 there. Then parseBody's own check becomes a redundant second line rather than the only one, and a new route cannot opt out by forgetting to call it.

title: The relative-time consolidation missed three call sites, and two of them reintroduce verbatim the exact two defects the shared module's own doc comment says it was written to fix
description:
lib/ui/relative-time.ts:22-31 documents a completed consolidation and names the defects it removed: "The single source for this format: previously ~10 near-identical copies had drifted (some read '0m ago' instead of 'just now', one never fell back to a date and read '92d ago' forever, and the date fallback varied between 'Aug 12' and '8/12/2026')." formatRelativeTime (:32-52) is the survivor, re-exported through components/admin/utils.ts:123 and components/assets/assets-types.ts:25 with "Canonical relative-time formatter" comments.

Three files still hand-roll it, and two of them are the two named defects:

1. components/admin/features/support-inbox.tsx:68 `timeAgo` ends at `return \`${Math.round(hrs / 24)}d ago\`` with no date fallback. That is the "read '92d ago' forever" bug, restored.
2. components/contact/support-tickets.tsx:65 `timeAgo` falls back at 30 days to `new Date(iso).toLocaleDateString()`, which renders "8/12/2026". That is the "varied between 'Aug 12' and '8/12/2026'" bug, restored; the canonical formatter falls back at 7 days to `toLocaleDateString("en-US", { month: "short", day: "numeric" })`, i.e. "Aug 12".

These two render the same objects. support-inbox.tsx is the staff view of a support ticket and support-tickets.tsx is the user's view of the same ticket, so one ticket's "last activity" reads "412d ago" to staff and "8/12/2026" to the user. The same pair also duplicates STATUS_STYLES and StatusBadge (support-inbox.tsx:79, support-tickets.tsx:89, identical bodies).

3. components/scanner/subdomain-discovery.tsx:92 defines a private `formatAge` even though lib/ui/relative-time.ts:8 exports one, and lib/ui/relative-time.ts:2-4 names this very component as its consumer: "shared by the result panels that show freshness (subdomain discovery, DNS records, port sweep). Matches the wording SubdomainDiscovery introduced." The two sibling panels do import it (components/scanner/port-scan-panel.tsx:22, components/scanner/dns-records-panel.tsx:24), and subdomain-discovery.tsx:22 imports formatRefreshAvailability from that same module in the same statement while shadowing formatAge. The bodies are currently identical, so this one is a live divergence risk rather than a current bug. A third, unrelated `formatAge(ageMs: number | null)` exists at components/admin/features/queue-status-utils.ts:41, so the name means two things.
impact: Staff triaging the support inbox see ages like "412d ago" that are unreadable as dates, on the one screen where knowing when a ticket last moved matters. The same ticket shows the user a different format. Beyond that, the consolidation is not actually done: the module presents itself as the single source and is not, so the next timestamp change is applied once and misses three screens, exactly as it did the last time.
recommendation: Delete components/admin/features/support-inbox.tsx:68 and components/contact/support-tickets.tsx:65 and import formatRelativeTime from @/lib/ui/relative-time in both. Delete components/scanner/subdomain-discovery.tsx:92 and use the exported formatAge already imported alongside formatRefreshAvailability at :22. Rename components/admin/features/queue-status-utils.ts:41 to formatAgeMs so the name is unambiguous. Hoist the shared StatusBadge and STATUS_STYLES out of the two support components into components/contact/ or a shared module.

title: Extends AUDIT-012#obs-09 with the success-shape half: GET responses use four different envelopes, three routes return a bare array, one paginated route names its count totalTeams while its three siblings use total, and lib/api/client.ts is imported by 2 files while 94 call fetch directly
description:
AUDIT-012#obs-09 inventoried the ERROR shapes (five of them, 117 of 155 routes bypassing ApiResponse/withErrorHandling). It did not cover the success side or the client side. I extracted the last success return from every GET handler in app/api (56 of them) and grouped them.

Envelopes in use:
  1. Named-key object, the majority: `{ shares }`, `{ teams }`, `{ tickets }`, `{ notifications }`, `{ feedback }`, `{ teammates }`, `{ invitations }`, `{ remediation }`, `{ summaries }`, `{ repos }`.
  2. Bare array, no envelope: app/api/v3/schedules/route.ts:60 (`result.rows`), app/api/v3/webhooks/route.ts:42 (`result.rows`), app/api/v3/badge/scans/route.ts (`scans`). A client cannot add a sibling field to these without a breaking change.
  3. `{ success: true, data: {...} }`: app/api/v3/checkout/verify-subscription/route.ts. Nothing else uses it, and app/api/v3/finding-types/route.ts uses `{ success: false, error }` for its failure but a bare object for its success, so `success` is not a reliable discriminator anywhere.
  4. Flat top-level fields with no envelope at all: app/api/v3/billing/route.ts, app/api/v3/config/client/route.ts, app/api/version/route.ts, app/api/v3/health/route.ts.

Pagination envelope keys diverge on one route: app/api/v3/admin/content/route.ts, app/api/v3/admin/email-logs/route.ts and app/api/v3/admin/error-logs/route.ts all return `{ <items>, page, totalPages, total }`, and app/api/v3/admin/teams/route.ts:71 returns `totalTeams` instead of `total` for the identical concept. components/admin/features/content-manager.tsx:107 reads `data.total || 0` to drive its "N total" footer; that pattern silently renders 0 against the teams endpoint, which is why components/admin/teams/teams-list.tsx:646 only consumes totalPages and drops the count. app/api/v3/admin/route.ts returns `total` with no page/totalPages at all.

The query-parameter side is, for the record, consistent: all seven paginated routes take `page` and `limit`, no route uses offset or cursor, so there is nothing to fix there.

On the client, lib/api/client.ts:44-49 is the shared reader that normalises `errorData.error` and falls back to the literal `API error: <status>`. It is imported by exactly 2 files under app/ and components/, while 94 files call `fetch(` directly and each re-implements its own `data.error || "Something went wrong"` handling. So the normalisation obs-09 recommends adopting has no adoption to build on.
impact: Every new client call site has to discover, per endpoint, whether the payload is the array itself, a named key, `data`, or flat fields, and whether the count is `total` or `totalTeams`. That is why the teams list drops its result count and why 94 files each carry their own error-unwrapping block. The three bare-array endpoints (schedules, webhooks, badge/scans) cannot gain pagination or a count without breaking their callers. Documented in app/docs/api, these inconsistencies are also the public API surface, so third-party integrators hit them too.
recommendation: Pick the named-key envelope as canonical, since it is already the majority, and write it down in app/docs/api. Fix the three cheap deviants first: wrap app/api/v3/schedules/route.ts:60 and app/api/v3/webhooks/route.ts:42 as `{ schedules }` / `{ webhooks }` (both have exactly one client each, in components/profile/tabs/developer/), rename app/api/v3/admin/teams/route.ts:71 `totalTeams` to `total`, and convert app/api/v3/checkout/verify-subscription/route.ts off the lone `{ success, data }` shape. Then extend lib/api/client.ts to return the unwrapped payload and migrate call sites by directory, starting with components/profile/ where nine of them already duplicate the same error block.

title: Every index is built without CONCURRENTLY and the migration rewrites scan_history twice inside one transaction, while the self-updater runs it against a still-serving app
description: runPlan wraps the entire plan in a single BEGIN/COMMIT (line 95 to line 134) because "half-migrated schemas are the worst-case outcome", and the file header notes CONCURRENTLY is deliberately avoided since it cannot run in a transaction. The 2.0.0 to 3.0.0 plan contains 18 CREATE TABLE, 48 ADD COLUMN, 17 CREATE INDEX and 18 dataUpdates, all under that one transaction. Two of the ADD COLUMNs force a full rewrite of scan_history and hold ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on it for the whole remaining transaction: `share_token_hash TEXT GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...) STORED` (2.0.0-to-3.0.0.mjs:608-615) and `public_id TEXT DEFAULT (replace(gen_random_uuid()::text, '-', ''))` (line 879-883), whose volatile default is evaluated once per existing row. A third, `UPDATE scan_history SET public_id = ... WHERE public_id IS NULL` (line 1059), is an unbounded UPDATE over the same table. The boot path has the same property without the transaction: all 103 CREATE INDEX / CREATE UNIQUE INDEX statements in instrumentation.ts are plain, taking a SHARE lock that blocks writes for the build, and the same two scan_history rewrites appear at instrumentation.ts:1284 and 2613. The self-updater runs db:migrate from inside the running app and explicitly does not restart it (app/api/v3/admin/updater/apply/route.ts:28), so the app is serving throughout.
impact: At the current production size (roughly 50 users) this is seconds, not minutes, so the practical cost today is a short stall rather than an outage. But every request that reads or writes scan_history or users blocks for the full duration of the migration transaction, with no timeout and no warning anywhere in the UI: the updater dialog tells the operator only that the server is not restarted, implying it keeps serving normally. The cost scales linearly with scan_history, which is the fastest-growing table in the product, so the same release flow gets worse every month with no signal until it is a real outage.
recommendation: Split the plan into a transactional DDL phase and a post-commit index phase, and run the CREATE INDEX steps outside the transaction with CONCURRENTLY (which requires per-statement error handling and a re-run path for INVALID indexes). Set `SET LOCAL lock_timeout` and `statement_timeout` at the start of the migration transaction so a blocked ACCESS EXCLUSIVE acquisition fails fast instead of queuing every request behind it. Add a warning to the updater dialog that db:migrate briefly locks the database.

title: Two tables exist only as lazy runtime DDL: staff_invites and admin_audit_log_archive are in no schema file, no migration, and no required-table check, and staff_invites re-runs its CREATE TABLE on every admin request
description: instrumentation.ts is documented as the canonical schema and contains 64 CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS statements. Two more tables exist that it never creates. (1) `staff_invites` is created by `ensureStaffInvitesTable()` (lib/admin/staff-invites.ts:33-48), whose own doc comment at :22-31 says it is "intentionally NOT called from instrumentation.ts directly" and instructs whoever wires the schema change to add the import there. That was never done: a repo-wide grep for `ensureStaffInvitesTable` finds it called only from the three handlers in app/api/v3/admin/staff-invites/route.ts (:75, :177, :216), never at boot. (2) `admin_audit_log_archive` is created by `ensureAuditLogArchiveTable()` (lib/database/audit-log-archive.ts:43-57), whose doc comment at :37-41 gives the same never-executed wiring instruction; the only real call site is inside `archiveAdminAuditLogBeforePurge` at :77, which runs it against the transactional client of the nightly cleanup pass (lib/database/cleanup.ts:308), so DDL executes inside the long cleanup transaction on every run. Neither table appears anywhere in scripts/create-fresh-db/ or scripts/migrate/ (grep for both names in those directories returns nothing), and neither is in lib/database/required-tables.ts, so the boot-time verification at instrumentation.ts:3515-3543 and GET /api/v3/health both report a healthy schema on a database that is missing them. The public accept endpoint app/api/v3/auth/staff-invite/[token]/route.ts queries `staff_invites` at :57, :104 and :208 without ever calling ensureStaffInvitesTable first.
impact: `npm run db:create` and `npm run db:migrate` both produce a database that is missing these two tables, and nothing reports it. The staff-invite feature only works because its admin route happens to create the table as a side effect of the first request. That side effect also means every GET, POST and DELETE on /api/v3/admin/staff-invites executes one CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS plus two CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS against the system catalogs before doing any work, which is the same per-request DDL antipattern AUDIT-003#misc-01 reported for ai/conversations and that was fixed there. Anyone reading instrumentation.ts to understand the schema, or diffing it against a production database, gets a wrong answer for two tables.
recommendation: Move both CREATE TABLE statements into instrumentation.ts's boot block, as each module's own doc comment already asks: put staff_invites next to team_invites (after line 917) and admin_audit_log_archive next to admin_audit_log (after line 579). Keep the ensure* functions but call them once at boot and delete the calls from app/api/v3/admin/staff-invites/route.ts:75, :177 and :216 and from lib/database/audit-log-archive.ts:77 so no DDL runs on a request path or inside the cleanup transaction. Add both names to lib/database/required-tables.ts, and add the DDL to scripts/create-fresh-db and the current migration version so a fresh install and a migrated install agree.

title: The root package.json `overrides` block that pins postcss, sharp and brace-expansion does not apply to extension/ or marketing/, so a security pin added at the root silently leaves the shipped extension unpatched
description: `package.json:137` declares an `overrides` block that pins `postcss: "8.5.26"`, `sharp: "^0.35.0"`, `brace-expansion@1: "1.1.18"`, `brace-expansion@2: "2.1.4"`, and the four @typescript-eslint packages. npm `overrides` are scoped to the manifest that declares them and to that install tree only. `extension/` and `marketing/` are not npm workspaces (the root manifest has no `workspaces` field) and each has its own independent `package-lock.json`, so none of those pins reaches them. The divergence is already visible in the resolved trees: postcss is 8.5.26 in the root lock (the pinned value) and 8.5.23 in `extension/package-lock.json`, even though the extension still runs postcss on every build (`extension/vite.config.ts:39` sets `css.postcss.plugins: []`, which selects an empty plugin list, not a bypass of the postcss pipeline). brace-expansion resolves to 1.1.18 plus 5.0.9 at the root, 2.1.4 in extension, and 1.1.18 plus 2.1.4 in marketing. esbuild is 0.25.12 in extension and 0.28.1 in marketing. All of those specific versions happen to be past their known advisories today, so nothing is exploitable right now; the finding is the mechanism. The root overrides exist precisely because someone reacted to an advisory by pinning a transitive package, and that reflex will not protect the artifact that ships to users' browsers.
impact: The next time a transitive advisory is handled by adding an entry to the root `overrides` block, the browser extension keeps the vulnerable version and nothing reports it (see subdeps-02: the extension tree is not audited or watched at all). The operator will reasonably believe the pin covered the repo.
recommendation: Either convert `extension` into an npm workspace of the root manifest so one lockfile and one `overrides` block govern both trees, or, if the separate lockfile is deliberate (CI caches `extension/package-lock.json` separately at `.github/workflows/ci.yml:129`), add an `overrides` block to `extension/package.json` and add a short note to the root `overrides` block at `package.json:137` saying that every entry added there must be mirrored into `extension/package.json`.

title: The extension builds with Vite 6.4.3, two majors behind the supported window (latest 8.2.2, previous 7.3.6), and that toolchain emits the IIFE injected into every page the user visits
category: unsupported major on the build toolchain
description: `extension/package.json:37` declares `"vite": "^6.4.3"`, resolved to 6.4.3 in `extension/package-lock.json`. `npm view vite dist-tags` returns `latest: 8.2.2` and `previous: 7.3.6`, so Vite 6 is neither the current nor the previous major and is outside the line that receives backported fixes. The same tree carries esbuild 0.25.12 (marketing's independent tree already resolves 0.28.1) and archiver 7.0.1 against latest 8.0.0 per `npm outdated --json`. This is not an ordinary application dependency: `extension/scripts/build.mjs:44` and `:59` call Vite's programmatic `build()` twice, once for the three HTML pages and once per entry for `background/service-worker.ts` and `content/detector.ts`, and those two IIFE bundles are what the manifest injects as the MV3 service worker and as a `content_scripts` entry matching `<all_urls>` (`extension/manifest/chrome.json:47`). The same `build.mjs` output is what `extension/scripts/package.mjs` zips and what `.github/workflows/release.yml:147` builds and attaches to the GitHub release for Chrome Web Store and AMO upload. Because the root's own Vite (8.2.2, pulled in transitively by vitest 4.1.11) is a completely separate install tree, the repo already proves Vite 8 works here for the rest of the codebase; only the extension is stuck. Combined with subdeps-02 (no Dependabot and no audit on this manifest), nothing will ever nudge this forward.
impact: The one toolchain that generates browser-privileged code for real users is on a major that will not get security fixes, and no automation watches it. A build-chain compromise or a Rollup/esbuild output bug lands directly in an extension with all-URLs content-script access, and the upgrade path only gets longer the further behind it drifts (a 6 to 8 jump is two sets of breaking changes at once).
recommendation: Bump `extension/package.json:37` to `"vite": "^8.2.2"` and `"archiver": "^8.0.0"` at line 33, run `npm install` inside `extension/` only (its lockfile is separate from the root's, so this does not touch the root package-lock), then verify `npm run build:chrome && npm run build:firefox` still emits classic-script `background.js` and `content.js` with no top-level imports, which is the invariant documented in `extension/vite.config.ts:9`. Load both unpacked builds once before releasing.

title: marketing/ is entirely gitignored, so 401 packages, a 270 MB downloaded Chromium and a local .env full of credentials sit inside the repo tree with zero supply-chain visibility
category: untracked dependency tree inside the repo
description: First, the question that sets the severity of everything else here: marketing/ is NOT built or deployed as part of the product. `.gitignore:74` ignores the whole `marketing/` directory, `git ls-files marketing` returns 0 files, and no workflow, `next.config`, `vercel.json`, `tsconfig.json` or root script references it (grep for "marketing" across `.github`, `next.config.*`, `vercel.json`, `package.json`, `tsconfig.json` returns nothing). It is a standalone Remotion asset-generation project run manually on the maintainer's machine. Its dependencies therefore carry no production risk. What they do carry is a blind spot. Because `marketing/package.json` and `marketing/package-lock.json` are untracked, Dependabot cannot see them (it needs a committed manifest), `npm audit` at the root never walks into them, and the CycloneDX SBOM built from the Docker image (`.github/workflows/docker-publish.yml:82`) excludes them. Measured on disk: `marketing/node_modules` is 648 MB across 401 lockfile entries, of which `node_modules/.remotion/chrome-headless-shell/win64/` is 270 MB, a Chromium headless-shell binary that @remotion/renderer downloads over the network on first render rather than at install, and `@remotion/compositor-win32-x64-msvc` is another 29 MB of native binary including a bundled `ffmpeg.exe`. That tree executes on a machine where `marketing/.env` (365 bytes, present on disk, correctly ignored) holds credentials, and `marketing/package.json:31` wires `npm run audio` to `node scripts/make-audio.mjs`, which is what consumes them. The tree is also drifting on its own: React 19.2.3 against the root's 19.2.8, @types/react 19.2.7 against 19.2.18, prettier 3.8.1 against 3.9.6, eslint 9.19.0 against the root's 10.9.0.
impact: Nobody is watching 401 packages plus two downloaded native binaries that run with full user privileges on the maintainer's workstation next to a credentials file. A malicious postinstall or a compromised Remotion transitive release would execute there and nothing in the repo's security automation would notice, because from git's point of view the directory does not exist. Separately, the project is unreproducible: no other contributor can restore the exact tree that rendered the shipped videos, since the lockfile is not in git.
recommendation: Decide which of the two this is. If marketing/ should stay private, move it out of the repo working tree entirely (a sibling directory or its own repo) so it is not silently inside a scanned checkout, and keep a lockfile under version control wherever it lands. If it should stay in place, narrow `.gitignore:74` from `marketing/` to `marketing/node_modules/`, `marketing/out/`, `marketing/.env`, and `marketing/public/` so that `marketing/package.json` and `marketing/package-lock.json` become tracked, then add a `directory: "/marketing"` block to `.github/dependabot.yml`. Either way, document that the 270 MB chrome-headless-shell arrives on first `remotion render`, not on `npm install`.

title: The only regression guard for the scanner's per-check error isolation never makes a check throw, and its sole assertion is .not.toThrow()
category: test would pass with the feature removed
description: tests/lib/scanner/engine.test.ts:72 is titled "does not let one throwing check take down the whole scan". Its body builds a pathological body string (`"<".repeat(5000) + "html".repeat(1000)`) and asserts exactly one thing: `expect(() => runSyncChecks(...)).not.toThrow()`. No detector in the run is made to throw: a grep for `throw new Error` in that file returns nothing, and no detector is stubbed or injected. The feature it is supposed to guard is the pair of per-check try/catch blocks in lib/scanner/engine.ts at lines 169 to 172 and 186 to 198 (the file's own comment at line 131 calls them "the per-check try/catch below"). The exact mutation the test does not catch: delete both try/catch wrappers in lib/scanner/engine.ts, and the test still passes, because none of the 800-plus registered detectors throws on that particular input. It also does not assert that findings are still produced, so a mutation that makes runSyncChecks return `{ findings: [] }` unconditionally also passes.
impact: The per-check try/catch is what stops one bad regex or one bad detector from aborting an entire scan. If it is removed or narrowed during a refactor, the suite says nothing, and the symptom in production is a scan that returns a 500 or an empty result for every user whose page happens to trip the throwing detector. The test also carries a documented flake: its own comment at lines 65 to 70 records that the default 5s timeout "has been observed to flake under a full parallel suite run", which is why it now runs with a 20s override, so a very expensive test is buying an assertion that cannot fail.
recommendation: In tests/lib/scanner/engine.test.ts, register a deliberately throwing detector (or vi.spyOn one entry of ALL_INLINE_DETECTORS to throw) and assert two things: that runSyncChecks still returns, and that the findings from the other categories are still present. Keep the pathological-input case as a separate, honestly named smoke test.

title: Nothing limits requests per TARGET, nothing verifies ownership for an ordinary scan, and a wildcard robots.txt Disallow is deliberately ignored
description: Every limiter in the codebase is keyed on the caller, never on the victim. Grepping `key: \`` across app/api shows the rate-limit keys are all `${userId}` or `${ip}` (plus two per-account keys for login/signup email); there is no `${hostname}`/`${rootDomain}` bucket anywhere, and lib/rate-limiting/ contains no target-side concept at all. Domain-ownership verification (isUrlOwnedByUser, lib/domains/scope.ts) is applied only when the request asks for active probes or a port scan (app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:310-324); an ordinary scan, crawl, bulk scan or schedule against any domain the caller does not own is permitted. checkAccessRules is an operator-maintained blacklist consulted on 5 of the scan entry points and absent from the two discover endpoints and the scheduled worker (see abuse-01, abuse-04); there is no shipped blocklist of sensitive target classes (.gov, financial, the product's own infrastructure). The crawler's robots.txt handling is deliberately partial: lib/scanner/crawl-discovery.ts:243 requires `value && value !== "*" && uaLower.includes(value.toLowerCase())`, so a site's `User-agent: *` / `Disallow: /` has no effect and only a group naming VulnRadar specifically is honoured (:207-216 documents this as intentional); `crawl-delay` is matched at :253 purely to mark that a rule line was seen and is otherwise discarded. On volume: one single-URL scan sends roughly 40-60 requests to the target (checkExposedFiles alone is ~23, per the comment at lib/scanner/async-checks.ts:2724 and :2799, plus checkGraphQLIntrospection up to 4 and the other live-fetch checks), and a crawl multiplies that by the page count (25 free, up to 250 elite).
impact: VulnRadar will point itself at any third party on request, at a rate limited only by how many accounts the requester creates, and a site owner has no working way to opt out: the standard wildcard robots.txt directive is ignored by design, crawl-delay is discarded, and there is no abuse contact path enforced in-product. A coordinated set of free accounts converges on one victim with no server-side signal that anything unusual is happening, and every request originates from VulnRadar's IP, so the operator absorbs the abuse reports and the blocklisting.
recommendation: Add a per-target bucket to lib/rate-limiting/ keyed on the registrable domain (extractRootDomain from lib/scanner/root-domain.ts) and check it in every scan entry point alongside the existing per-user check, so total inbound-to-one-victim volume is bounded across all accounts. Ship a default access-rules seed covering .gov/.mil and the deployment's own hostnames. Honour `User-agent: *` Disallow rules and crawl-delay in lib/scanner/crawl-discovery.ts for unverified domains, keeping the current ignore-wildcard behaviour only for a domain the caller has verified via isUrlOwnedByUser.

title: Every PUBLIC_PATHS entry skips the CSRF check entirely, including POST /api/v3/auth/login and the session-authenticated POST /api/v3/badge/site
description: middleware.ts computes `isPublicPath` at line 265 and, when it matches, returns at line 291 -- 25 lines BEFORE the `if (pathname.startsWith("/api/v3/") && !isExemptFromCsrf(pathname))` block at line 316 that calls enforceCsrf(). So the narrow, deliberately-curated exemption list in isExemptFromCsrf (line 350, which AUDIT-010#security-03 tightened from a prefix match to exact paths) is not the real exemption list: PUBLIC_PATHS is, and it is much wider. It exempts POST /api/v3/auth/login, /signup, /forgot-password, /reset-password, /accept-tos, /2fa/verify, /2fa/email-send, /verify-email, /resend-verification (lib/config/public-paths.ts:21-28), the prefixes "/api/v3/auth/discord", "/api/v3/auth/oauth", "/api/v3/badge", "/api/v3/shared", "/api/v3/stripe/setup-webhook", "/api/v3/stripe/setup-products", and "/api/v3/account/unsubscribe". Two concrete consequences. (1) Login CSRF: parseBody (lib/api/api-utils.ts:210-221) falls through to `request.json()` for any content-type that is not multipart/form-data, so a cross-origin `<form enctype="text/plain">` whose single field name is `{"email":"attacker@x","password":"p","z":"` and value is `"}` posts valid JSON to /api/v3/auth/login; the handler at app/api/v3/auth/login/route.ts:274 calls createSession(), whose Set-Cookie the browser stores, and the victim is now signed into the attacker's account. (2) app/api/v3/badge/site/route.ts:14 is a session-cookie-authenticated POST that lives under the "/api/v3/badge" prefix (lib/config/public-paths.ts:154) and reads its body with `req.json()` at line 19 -- the same text/plain form reaches it and mints host_badges rows on a logged-in victim's account.
impact: The login-CSRF instance is the same class of attack as auth-01 and reaches the same outcome (victim silently operating inside the attacker's account) through the password endpoint rather than Discord, so fixing auth-01 alone does not close it. Structurally, the bigger problem is that adding a path to PUBLIC_PATHS -- which reads as 'no login required' -- silently also removes CSRF protection, so any future session-authenticated mutating route added under a public prefix (as /api/v3/badge/site already is) becomes forgeable with no code review signal.
recommendation: In middleware.ts, hoist the CSRF block above the `if (isPublicPath)` return: move lines 316-321 (the `pathname.startsWith("/api/v3/")` + enforceCsrf call) to just after `const hasBearerToken` is computed and before the public-path branch at line 273, so isExemptFromCsrf becomes the single authority on what is exempt. Nothing in PUBLIC_PATHS legitimately needs the exemption -- every same-origin fetch from the app sends an Origin header -- and the three that genuinely do (Stripe webhook, Discord callback, demo-scan) are already listed in isExemptFromCsrf.

title: Session tokens are stored raw in the database: sessions.id IS the cookie value, unlike every other token in the codebase
category: secret stored in plaintext at rest
description: createSession generates 32 CSPRNG bytes (lib/auth/auth.ts:32-34), inserts them verbatim as the primary key at line 57 (`INSERT INTO sessions (id, ...) VALUES ($1, ...)`), and sets that same string as the cookie value at line 63. getSession looks it up with `WHERE s.id = $1` on the raw cookie (line 93). The file's own hashSessionId comment (lines 379-390) states the situation plainly: 'The `id` column is not a surrogate key: it is the literal bearer token stored in the httpOnly session cookie'. Every other bearer secret in this codebase is hashed before storage precisely so a database read cannot be replayed: password-reset tokens (app/api/v3/auth/forgot-password/route.ts:19,87), email-verification tokens (lib/auth/email-verification.ts:31), staff-invite tokens (app/api/v3/auth/staff-invite/[token]/route.ts:34), share tokens (AUDIT-004#secrets-01), and email 2FA codes, which even get a per-row salt (app/api/v3/auth/login/route.ts:222). API keys and TOTP seeds are at least AES-256-GCM encrypted (lib/auth/crypto.ts). Sessions are the only credential left in plaintext, and they are the highest-value one: lib/auth/impersonation.ts:103 also writes a second raw session id into the `imp_return_session` cookie.
impact: Any read of the sessions table -- a leaked backup, a read replica, a blind SQL injection anywhere in 155 API routes, or a support engineer with psql -- yields directly replayable, ready-to-use session cookies for every signed-in user, including admins, for up to SESSION_TIMEOUT_DAYS (7). No further work is needed by the attacker: paste the value into a `vulnradar_session` cookie. Every other token class in the app is already immune to exactly this, so the exposure is concentrated entirely in the one place it hurts most.
recommendation: Store `sha256(token)` as sessions.id and keep the raw value only in the cookie. In lib/auth/auth.ts: hash in createSession before the INSERT (line 57) and return the raw token; hash the cookie value in getSession before the SELECT (line 93) and in destroySession (line 240); hashSessionId already exists and can be reused as the digest function. The three other places that compare a raw cookie to a stored id need the same treatment: listUserSessions/findUserSessionByHash (lines 415-450, which currently hash the stored value a second time), app/api/v3/auth/sessions/route.ts:57's `s.id === currentSessionId`, and lib/auth/impersonation.ts:66-72 and :113-128. Ship it with a migration that truncates the sessions table (a forced re-login) rather than trying to convert rows in place.

title: Creating an API key requires no re-authentication, so a stolen session mints a credential that outlives 'sign out everywhere'
description: POST /api/v3/keys (app/api/v3/keys/route.ts:32) checks only `getSession()` and a plan limit before calling generateApiKey (lib/api/api-keys.ts:65), which returns the raw `vr_live_...` key in the response body. There is no current-password check and no rate limit on the endpoint. Every other sensitive action in this codebase does gate on re-auth: email and password change (app/api/v3/auth/update/route.ts:70-115, with its own strict `profile-reauth` login bucket), enabling TOTP (app/api/v3/auth/2fa/setup/route.ts:107-123), enabling/disabling email 2FA (app/api/v3/auth/2fa/email-setup/route.ts:258, :325), disabling 2FA (app/api/v3/auth/2fa/disable/route.ts:51), regenerating backup codes (app/api/v3/auth/2fa/backup-codes/route.ts:178), and deleting the account (app/api/v3/account/delete/route.ts:70). The API key is the one credential of the set that is not merely long-lived but independent of the session that created it: DELETE /api/v3/auth/sessions (app/api/v3/auth/sessions/route.ts:62) deletes every sessions row and does not touch api_keys, and neither does a password change (app/api/v3/auth/update/route.ts:343-350 clears sessions and device_trust only).
impact: An attacker holding a session cookie for a few seconds -- an unlocked shared machine, a session lifted from a backup per auth-07, a support handoff -- creates an API key, reads it out of the JSON response, and keeps full scan/history/delete access on that account indefinitely. Every recovery action the victim knows about (sign out everywhere, change password, rotate 2FA) leaves the key working, and the only signal is one 'API key created' email that a user who did not create it is likely to dismiss. The key is also silently upgraded to the plan's real daily quota (line 93), so the cost lands on the victim.
recommendation: Gate POST /api/v3/keys the same way app/api/v3/auth/update/route.ts:75-115 gates a sensitive change: require `currentPassword` in the body, verify it against `users.password_hash` behind a `keys-create:${userId}:${ip}` bucket using RATE_LIMITS.login, and skip only the password check (never the rate limit) for the null-hash OAuth-only case. Wire the field into the create-key modal in components/profile/tabs/developer/. Separately, add `UPDATE api_keys SET revoked_at = NOW() WHERE user_id = $1` to the DELETE /api/v3/auth/sessions handler, or at minimum surface active keys on that confirmation screen, so 'sign out everywhere' means what users think it means.

title: GET /api/v3/admin?section=user-detail has no permission gate, so the ops role reads any user's PII, sessions and IPs without VIEW_USERS
description: app/api/v3/admin/route.ts's GET gates only on requireStaff() at :81, which passes for any role at or above STAFF_ROLE_HIERARCHY.support = 10 (lib/config/client-constants.ts:39-49; ops/billing/security_analyst/content_manager are all 20). Two of its five sections then check nothing further: `section === "user-detail"` at :130 and the default stats+user-list branch at :325. The audit and active-admins sections DO gate, on hasStaffPermission(session.role, VIEW_AUDIT_LOG) at :249 and :294, which is the pattern the others are missing. user-detail returns, for any userId: email, role, plan, stripe_customer_id, subscription_status, google/github/discord identity columns, every active session row with ip_address and user_agent (:180-183), every api_keys row with prefix/limits (:168-171), webhooks, scheduled scans and internal admin notes. The ops role's grant list (lib/auth/permissions-client.ts:181-191) contains neither VIEW_USERS nor VIEW_USER_SESSIONS; billing (:145) and content_manager (:170) hold VIEW_USERS but not VIEW_USER_SESSIONS, yet all of them receive the session IP list. AUDIT-011#drift-18 flagged the matching UI cards in user-detail-panel.tsx; this is the API behind them, which a direct request reaches regardless of what the UI renders.
impact: Any of the four narrow specialist staff roles - which exist precisely so an ops or content person can reach one admin tab without user data - can read every user's email, billing identifiers, linked social accounts and last-known IP addresses by calling one URL. On a ~50-user production instance that is the entire user base's PII available to a role the operator deliberately scoped away from it.
recommendation: In app/api/v3/admin/route.ts, gate the user-detail branch (:130) and the default user-list branch (:325) on hasStaffPermission(session.role, STAFF_PERMISSIONS.VIEW_USERS) the same way :249 gates on VIEW_AUDIT_LOG, and drop the `activeSessions` key from the user-detail response (or the whole `sessionsRes` query) unless the caller also holds VIEW_USER_SESSIONS. Add the missing VIEW_BADGES gate to the badges branch at :281 while there.

title: Staff invite emails link to /staff-invite/[token], a page that does not exist, so no staff invite can ever be accepted
description: app/api/v3/admin/staff-invites/route.ts:134 builds `const inviteLink = `${APP_URL}/staff-invite/${token}`` and emails it (staffInviteEmail at :135). There is no app/staff-invite directory anywhere under app/ - the only matches for "staff-invite" are the two API route directories - so that URL 404s. The backing API pair app/api/v3/auth/staff-invite/[token]/route.ts exists and is fully implemented (GET validates a token without consuming it, POST accepts it and promotes or creates the account in one transaction), and its header at :22-30 calls itself "Public accept endpoints for a staff invite" - yet it is also absent from PUBLIC_PATHS, so even a hand-built page would be 307'd to /login for the invitee who has no account yet, which is the whole point of an invite. The admin-side UI is shipped and working: components/admin/staff/staff-list.tsx:117-127 lists pending invites and the modal creates them.
impact: Every staff invite an admin sends produces an email whose only call to action is a 404. There is no fallback path: the accept endpoints have no other caller. Adding staff therefore still requires an admin to edit the target account's role by hand in the admin panel, and the invite table accumulates rows nobody can act on.
recommendation: Build app/staff-invite/[token]/page.tsx: GET /api/v3/auth/staff-invite/[token] to show the invited email and role, then POST to accept (with a password field when the account does not exist yet, matching that route's POST contract). Add "/staff-invite" and "/api/v3/auth/staff-invite" to PUBLIC_PATHS in lib/config/public-paths.ts, beside the existing ROUTES.TEAMS_JOIN entry at :191 which exists for the identical "invitee has no account yet" reason.

title: Twenty docs pages are client components purely to drive a TOC scroll-spy, serializing 12,492 lines / 518 KB of static prose into the browser bundle
description: Every page under app/docs/ carries "use client" (20 files, 12,492 lines, 517,607 bytes of source measured directly). The only client-side behaviour in almost all of them is two effects: one registering a static tocItems array with the docs context (app/docs/setup/page.tsx:44-47) and one wiring an IntersectionObserver scroll-spy (app/docs/setup/page.tsx:49-67). Everything else in the file is static JSX prose. app/docs/architecture/page.tsx:41, app/docs/triage/page.tsx:156, app/docs/api/page.tsx:1026 and the rest are byte-identical copies of the same two effects. The context that consumes them, components/docs/docs-shell.tsx, is already a client component, so the sidebar and TOC would keep working if the page bodies were server components. app/docs/config/page.tsx compounds it: at line 14 it imports SETTINGS_REGISTRY from lib/config/registry.ts (3,199 lines) into a client component just to render a static settings table, which is why static/chunks/6027-6257bc191d11b0fb.js (72 KB raw / 18 KB gzipped, containing setting keys, defaults and descriptions) ships to the browser on /docs/config. Measured route totals from the committed build, layout chunks included: /docs/config/page 931 KB raw JS, /docs/api/page 862 KB, /docs/setup/page 858 KB (258 KB gzipped).
impact: Pages that are pure documentation, and are the pages most worth ranking (docs-shell.tsx's own comment says so), pay full client-component cost: every paragraph is serialized twice, once as HTML and again as React element JS. React hydrates thousands of static nodes on pages where nothing is interactive, and /docs/config additionally ships the whole admin settings registry to anonymous readers.
recommendation: Extract the two effects into one small client leaf, e.g. `components/docs/docs-toc-spy.tsx` exporting `<DocsTocSpy items={tocItems} />` that does the setTocItems registration and the IntersectionObserver, then delete "use client" from all 20 app/docs/*/page.tsx files and render `<DocsTocSpy items={tocItems} />` at the top of each. For app/docs/config/page.tsx that also moves the SETTINGS_REGISTRY import (line 14) back to the server, removing chunk 6027 from the route.

title: The host-report trend request cannot start until the host report resolves, because the chart is mounted inside the result-gated subtree
description: app/host/[hostname]/page.tsx is a client component whose entire body is gated on a useEffect fetch. The effect at line 64-85 calls `fetch(API.HOST(hostname))`; the report subtree is rendered only under `{!loading && !error && result && (` at line 179; `<DangerScoreTrend hostname={...} />` is passed as the afterSummary prop at line 277, inside that gate. DangerScoreTrend then runs its own effect (components/host/danger-score-trend.tsx:43-59) calling `fetch(API.HOST_TREND(hostname))`. The two endpoints are independent -- the trend route keys only off the hostname in the URL -- so request B is serialized behind request A for no reason. And because the page is "use client" with no server-side data fetch, the first paint for a visitor or a crawler is the skeleton at line ~150 until ~442 KB gzipped of JS parses and one round trip completes.
impact: Public host reports, which are indexable pages, show a skeleton until JS has downloaded, parsed, and completed a round trip, and then wait for a second serialized round trip before the trend chart can appear. LCP on the route is two sequential network hops plus a large parse, and crawlers that do not execute JS see no report content at all.
recommendation: Fetch the host report on the server. Convert app/host/[hostname]/page.tsx into a server component that awaits the same query the /api/v3/host/[hostname] route runs, issue the host and trend queries with `Promise.all`, and pass both down; keep only the interactive pieces (copy button, issue selection, back button) as client leaves. If a full conversion is too large, at minimum hoist the trend fetch out of DangerScoreTrend into the page's existing effect so both requests start together.

title: /changelog ships the entire 304 KB changelog dataset to the browser (259 KB chunk, 89 KB gzipped) to render four releases
description: components/changelog/changelog-list.tsx is "use client" and imports CHANGELOG from lib/changelog/data at line 7. lib/changelog/data.ts is 304,458 bytes / 4,636 lines of release records. Because the importer is a client component, the whole array is serialized into the route's client chunk: .next/static/chunks/app/changelog/page-73e8592bdfbd7e4b.js is 259 KB raw / 89,359 bytes gzipped, and the route totals 1,067 KB raw / 337 KB gzipped, second only to /host. The component then renders `INITIAL_BATCH = 4` releases (line 13) and reveals four more at a time via an IntersectionObserver sentinel. The page shell around it (app/changelog/page.tsx) is already a server component, so nothing forces the data to the client.
impact: Anyone opening /changelog downloads 89 KB gzipped of release history to see four entries, and the payload grows with every release appended per the project's own changelog-per-change rule. On a phone connection this is several seconds of transfer and parse before the first four entries paint.
recommendation: Keep lib/changelog/data on the server: in app/changelog/page.tsx slice CHANGELOG server-side and pass the first page of releases plus a total count into ChangelogList as props, and serve later batches from a small route handler (or a server action) that the existing IntersectionObserver sentinel calls. Alternatively render the whole list server-side as static HTML and keep only the collapse/expand behaviour client-side.

title: The notification bell and the site-notification banner both GET /api/v3/notifications/active with identical parameters on every page load, then each filter the same payload client-side
description: components/shared/site-notifications.tsx:674-706 (SiteNotificationsWrapper, mounted at app/layout.tsx:188) builds `?authenticated=..&staff=..` and fetches /api/v3/notifications/active, then keeps only type banner/modal/toast. components/shared/notification-center.tsx:290-319 builds the same two params, fetches the same URL, and keeps only type bell -- and re-polls it on setInterval every clientConfig.notificationPollIntervalMs (default CONFIG_NOTIFICATION_POLL_INTERVAL_MS = 300000, lib/config/config-values.ts:1097). A second interval at components/shared/notification-center.tsx:344 polls API.NOTIFICATIONS on the same schedule. So every page load issues two identical requests for one payload, and every open tab keeps one of them cycling forever.
impact: Every page view in the app doubles the request count and the database work for site notifications, including anonymous visitors on the public marketing pages (the wrapper runs regardless of sign-in state). The duplication is invisible in normal use, which is exactly why it will not be noticed as traffic grows.
recommendation: Fetch /api/v3/notifications/active once and share it. Move the fetch into a small SWR hook (e.g. lib/hooks/use-active-notifications.ts) keyed on the `authenticated`/`staff` params, have both SiteNotificationsWrapper (components/shared/site-notifications.tsx:687) and NotificationCenter (components/shared/notification-center.tsx:297) consume it, and keep the type filtering where it is. SWR's dedupingInterval then collapses the two calls into one and the existing 5-minute refresh becomes a single revalidation.

title: No poller anywhere in the app pauses when the tab is hidden: there is not one visibilitychange or document.hidden reference in the codebase
description: Grepping visibilitychange and document.hidden across app/, components/ and lib/ returns zero matches. Every recurring timer therefore keeps firing in a backgrounded tab: components/shared/notification-center.tsx:314 and :344 (two polls of /api/v3/notifications/active and API.NOTIFICATIONS every 300,000 ms by default), app/dashboard/page.tsx:140 (scan status, 2,000 ms, up to 16 minutes), app/browser/[id]/page.tsx:327 (browser session logs at LOGS_POLL_MS) and :202 (a 1,000 ms clock tick), components/admin/features/backup-manager.tsx:106 (2,000 ms), components/admin/features/updater-manager.tsx:171 (2,000 ms), components/admin/features/queue-status-manager.tsx:65 (45,000 ms), components/scanner/subdomain-discovery.tsx:202. Browsers throttle setTimeout/setInterval in hidden tabs to roughly 1/minute after a delay, but they do not stop fetches that a still-scheduled timer issues, and the 45 s and 300 s pollers are already slower than the throttle floor so they run essentially unthrottled.
impact: Users who leave the dashboard, an admin panel, or any page with the notification bell open in a background tab keep issuing authenticated, database-backed requests indefinitely. For an operator this shows up as a persistent request floor proportional to open tabs rather than to active users, and it is the kind of load that only becomes visible after the user base grows.
recommendation: Add a shared hook, e.g. lib/hooks/use-visible-interval.ts, that wraps setInterval and clears/restarts on document visibilitychange, and use it at components/shared/notification-center.tsx:314 and :344, components/admin/features/queue-status-manager.tsx:65, components/admin/features/backup-manager.tsx:106 and components/admin/features/updater-manager.tsx:171. For the fast pollers that track a real job (dashboard scan status, browser session logs) keep them running but back the interval off while hidden rather than stopping outright.

title: Client-side render crashes are logged only to the visitor's own browser console, while app/error.tsx tells them "This has been logged"
description: Every error boundary in the app reports into the browser only. app/error.tsx:21-23 is `useEffect(() => { console.error(\`[${APP_NAME}] Unhandled error:\`, error); }, [error])`; app/global-error.tsx:19-21, app/dashboard/error.tsx:24-25, app/admin/error.tsx:14-15, app/history/error.tsx:14-15 and app/profile/error.tsx are all the same one-liner. lib/database/error-log-capture.ts's installErrorLogCapture wraps console.error on the server only, from instrumentation.ts's register() (see its file header at :1-17), so none of those calls ever reach system_error_logs. There is no client-error reporting endpoint anywhere under app/api (no route matching error/telemetry/report other than the admin read-only viewers app/api/v3/admin/error-logs and email-logs). Meanwhile app/error.tsx:58-61 renders the sentence "This has been logged. Try again, or come back once we have looked at it." and the error.digest panel at :63-90 only renders when `error.digest` exists, which for a client-only render error it does not.
impact: The operator has zero visibility into client-side breakage. This project's single most-reported production failure mode is stale-deploy chunk 404s served as text/html (see the deploy-chunk-mismatch history), which manifests exactly as a client-side throw, and none of it is recorded server-side. The user is simultaneously told the error was logged, which is false, and given no reference to quote to support.
recommendation: Add a small rate-limited POST /api/v3/client-errors that accepts `{ message, digest, route }`, console.errors it server-side (which routes it into system_error_logs via the existing wrapper), and call it from app/error.tsx:22 and app/global-error.tsx:20 alongside the existing console.error. Change the copy at app/error.tsx:59 to only claim the error was logged when a digest or a successful report exists.

title: No request or scan correlation id exists anywhere, and system_error_logs stores only a free-text message with no level, route, user, or scan column
description: The only structured error store is system_error_logs, created at instrumentation.ts:636-641 as `(id SERIAL, message TEXT, detail TEXT, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ)`. lib/database/error-log-capture.ts:169-173 inserts exactly `(message, detail)`, formed by string-joining whatever arguments a console.error call happened to pass. There is no level column (console.warn is not captured at all, only console.error at :137), no route, no user id, no scan id, and no request id. Nothing in the app generates a request id: no middleware.ts code sets or reads an x-request-id header, and the only `requestId` identifiers in the tree belong to unrelated features (app/api/v3/scan/discover/route.ts:96 for discovery progress, lib/browserbase/network-capture.ts:76 for CDP frames). GET /api/v3/admin/error-logs (app/api/v3/admin/error-logs/route.ts:37) can therefore only offer page/limit/free-text search over message and detail. The gap is visible in the product copy: components/scanner/dashboard-error-state.tsx:129 tells the user "The error is logged with the reference below" and no reference is ever rendered, because DashboardErrorState has no id prop at all (:22-33).
impact: When a user reports "my scan failed around 3pm", an operator cannot filter to that user or that scan. They grep free-form English across every console.error the process made, from 328 call sites, with a coalescing window and a 100-insert-per-minute cap (error-log-capture.ts:73-79) that can drop exactly the burst they are looking for. Any multi-hop failure (route -> executeScan -> a check -> safeFetch) produces several unrelated-looking rows with nothing tying them together.
recommendation: Add `level`, `route`, `user_id`, `scan_id` and `request_id` columns to system_error_logs in instrumentation.ts and populate them from an AsyncLocalStorage context set in middleware.ts (generate a request id there, echo it as x-request-id). Have lib/database/error-log-capture.ts read that context in the wrapper at :137. Thread scanId into the scanner's console.error calls. Then surface the id in components/scanner/dashboard-error-state.tsx so the sentence at :129 is true.

title: validateScanTarget does an uncached blocking dns.lookup on every call and is invoked 12-20 times per scan, all of it through the four-thread libuv pool
category: repeated blocking resolution on a shared threadpool
description: `validateScanTarget` resolves the target with `await lookup(hostname, { all: true })` (lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts:460) and caches nothing. `safeFetch` calls it once per request (line 584) and again on every redirect hop (line 746), and it is additionally called directly from app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:276, lib/scanner/checks/tls.ts:104/247/359, lib/scanner/async-checks.ts:2251/2732/3566/3648/3755, lib/scanner/active-probes/shared.ts:160, lib/scanner/active-probes/open-redirect.ts:155, lib/scanner/subdomain-auto.ts:99 and lib/scanner/page-screenshot.ts:199. A single scan of one host therefore resolves that host 12-20 times. Unlike `dns.resolve*`, `dns.lookup` is `getaddrinfo` and runs on the libuv threadpool, which defaults to 4 threads; nothing in the repo sets `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` (no occurrence anywhere outside node_modules), and that same pool serves `fs` and node:crypto's async KDFs.
impact: The scan pays 12-20 identical resolutions it could pay once. More importantly, concurrent scans queue on four OS threads: with a resolver that takes 100ms, eight simultaneous scans serialize their SSRF checks and also stall unrelated filesystem and crypto work in the same process. VulnRadar runs as one persistent Node process, so this is process-wide back-pressure, not per-request.
recommendation: Add a short-TTL (5-15s) in-process memo in front of `validateScanTarget` in lib/scanner/safe-fetch.ts keyed on hostname, returning the cached `SafetyCheckResult`. The TTL must stay short so the DNS-rebinding protection the function exists for is preserved -- a 10s window is still far tighter than a scan's own lifetime. Separately, set `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` in the Dockerfile/start script to something matched to the box (16 is a common default for I/O-heavy Node services).

title: The scan progress tracker writes two UPDATEs to scan_history per category, so a single scan does about 40 row rewrites of the widest table in the schema
description: `createProgressTracker`'s `onProgress` hook fires an `UPDATE scan_history SET current_category = $1, categories_total = $2 WHERE id = $3` on every "start" event (lib/scanner/scan-jobs.ts:120-127) and an `UPDATE scan_history SET categories_completed = $1, categories_total = $2 ...` on every "done" event (lines 131-138). The hook is invoked twice per category by `runSyncChecks` (lib/scanner/engine.ts:166 and :203) and twice per branch by `runAsyncChecksDetailed` (lib/scanner/async-checks.ts:4642 and :4644). `categoriesTotal` is `plannedSync.length + plannedAsync.length` (app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:339), which for a default full scan is roughly 16 sync categories plus 4-5 async branches -- about 40 UPDATEs per scan. Because Postgres is MVCC, each one writes a new version of a `scan_history` row that carries the `findings`, `summary`, `response_headers` and `result_meta` JSONB columns.
impact: About 40 dead tuples per scan on the largest table in the schema, plus 40 write round trips competing for the same 10-connection pool the scan's own reads use. On a crawl this is 40 x page count. It also inflates autovacuum work on the one table every list, dashboard and public page reads from.
recommendation: Coalesce progress writes in lib/scanner/scan-jobs.ts:113: keep the counters in memory and flush at most once every ~500ms (or only when `current_category` actually changes) with a single UPDATE, dropping the separate start/done writes. The status poll already runs on a 2s interval (AUDIT-011 scan-03), so sub-second progress precision buys nothing.

title: Four hot queries wrap an indexed column in a function or regex, so the index that exists for them can never be used
description: (a) app/api/v3/host/[hostname]/trend/route.ts:77-82 filters `WHERE is_public = true AND status = 'completed' AND url ~* $1`, with `$1` built as `^https?://(www\.)?<host>([:/?]|$)` at line 70. `~*` is not a b-tree-indexable operator, so `idx_scan_history_url_public_completed` (instrumentation.ts:2359) degrades to a full scan applying a case-insensitive regex to every row, then a sort, and only then `LIMIT 30`. The query also selects the full `findings` JSONB for those 30 rows. This is a public unauthenticated page. (b) app/api/v3/dashboard/route.ts:75 joins on `DATE(sh.scanned_at) = days.day` (see perf-06). (c) lib/domains/scope.ts:47-53 filters `($1 = domain OR $1 LIKE '%.' || domain)` -- the LIKE pattern is built from the column with the parameter on the left, which no b-tree can serve, so `idx_domains_domain_verified` (instrumentation.ts:3189) is unusable and every scan authorization check scans all verified domains across all tenants. (d) app/api/v3/admin/blocked-data/route.ts:60-83 and its DELETE twin at :124-135 apply `LOWER(REGEXP_REPLACE(sh.url, ...))` per row over all of scan_history before the `LIMIT 100`.
impact: Each of these reads the whole table where an index exists specifically to prevent that. (a) and (c) are the ones that matter operationally: (a) is on an unauthenticated route whose cost grows with total public scan volume, and (c) runs on the authorization gate for every active-probe or port-scan request.
recommendation: For (a), store the normalized host at scan time (a `host` column populated from lib/scanner/root-domain.ts, indexed) and filter `WHERE host = $1` instead of regexing the URL; also stop selecting `findings` there and project only title/severity. For (b), rewrite as a range predicate. For (c), store the registrable domain and each of its parent suffixes so the lookup becomes `domain = ANY($1::text[])`, which is indexable. For (d), the same normalized `host` column removes the REGEXP_REPLACE.

title: The root layout reads headers() for a CSP nonce, which forces all ~790 public SEO pages to be server-rendered per request with no static or ISR output
category: no static rendering anywhere in the app
description: `RootLayout` does `const nonce = (await headers()).get('x-nonce') ?? undefined` at app/layout.tsx:146. The comment above it (lines 139-145) states the consequence outright: this "forces this layout (and everything under it) into per-request dynamic rendering". app/checks/[id]/page.tsx repeats it at lines 29-31 -- `generateStaticParams` still enumerates the id space (line 34) but the pages are never actually prerendered. `getAllChecks()` returns the full check inventory (lib/seo/checks-content.ts:142), which is the ~754-page /checks tree, plus /checks/category/*, /docs, /finding-types, /host/* and the legal pages -- roughly 790 public routes, every one of which runs the full React server render on every single hit.
impact: Googlebot crawling the /checks tree, or any traffic to the SEO surface the project deliberately built for discovery, costs a full server render per page view with zero cache. The same CPU is shared with the scan engine's synchronous check loop (AUDIT-011 scan-06) in one Node process, so crawler traffic directly slows scans. It also means `next build` produces no static output for content that never changes between deploys.
recommendation: Move the nonce out of the layout's render. Either (a) have middleware.ts inject the nonce into the response HTML stream so the layout stays static, or (b) switch the CSP for the static content routes to a hash-based or `strict-dynamic`-with-no-nonce policy, and drop the `headers()` read from app/layout.tsx so /checks, /docs and the legal pages can be prerendered and revalidated on a long interval. Keep the nonce path for the authenticated app routes that genuinely need per-request rendering.

title: POST /api/v3/scan/bulk does roughly nine sequential database round trips per URL, up to 900-1000 in one request, and takes a row lock on the API key each time
description: The bulk route loops `for (let i = 0; i < urlsToScan.length; i++)` at app/api/v3/scan/bulk/route.ts:622 with every step awaited in order.
